title: Lifetime, RAII, and unique ownership
goal: Use constructor and destructor logs to trace object lifetime and transfer of sole ownership.

prerequisites.text: Modules 1–2: expressions, comparisons, types, references, and checked cin.
Follow the prerequisite links: cpp.unions-typedef-enums, cpp.standard-sequences. New constructs are introduced before the assignment.

sections.title: Lifetime and scope
paragraphs: A local variable is named inside its scope, while its resource exists until the object is destroyed. A log lets you observe destruction without reading a destroyed object.

Scope determines where a name is usable; lifetime determines when its object exists. A local object is normally destroyed on leaving its block, including via return. Copying its address outside does not keep the object alive.

An observer such as int*, a reference, span, or string_view neither releases an object nor extends its owner’s lifetime. Before use, establish that the object is alive and no owner operation has invalidated the address.

sections.title: A minimal constructor vocabulary
paragraphs: In struct Trace { explicit Trace(int n):id(n){} ~Trace(){} int id; }; the constructor has the type’s name and no return type. :id(n) initializes the field before the body. ~Trace is called when the object’s lifetime ends.

explicit prevents certain implicit conversions from a single argument. Here the structure is a small explained lifetime-log scaffold; the full treatment of encapsulation and special member functions remains in Module 5.
Trace{2} prints create 2 on entry to the inner block. Its destructor runs at the closing brace before the next print.

sections.title: Reverse destruction order
paragraphs: Order the create, destroy and end lines by the two scopes.

sections.title: RAII binds a resource to an object
paragraphs: RAII means an object acquires a resource during initialization and releases it in its destructor. vector manages a buffer, string manages text, and ofstream will later manage a file. Normal scope exit automatically triggers cleanup.

This is useful even without exceptions. It does not promise destructors will run after process termination or forced Worker cancellation. Saving a learner project and confirming a write are therefore separate interface actions.
With RAII, an object acquires the resource and its destructor releases it. Even an early return from scope destroys ordinary local owners.

sections.title: unique_ptr and make_unique
paragraphs: std::unique_ptr<T> from <memory> owns one T object; std::make_unique<T>(args) creates it and returns its owner. An empty pointer is false in a condition. p->value accesses the object’s field, while p.get() obtains a non-owning raw pointer.

Do not delete p.get() or create another owner from the same address. reset() without an argument releases the current object and empties the pointer. Any observers of that released object are then invalid.
make_unique creates the owner of Trace. get() supplies an observer for comparison, never a second owner that may delete it.

sections.title: Transferring ownership with move
paragraphs: std::move from <utility> permits a move; the call alone neither relocates memory nor destroys the object. auto q=std::move(p) move-constructs the unique_ptr: q becomes the owner and p becomes empty. Copying a unique_ptr is forbidden.

The T object retains its address during this ownership transfer. An observer remains usable while q owns the live object, but not after q.reset(). Other moved-from types are not necessarily empty unless their documentation promises it.
After move, two independent facts are checked: the previous unique_ptr is empty, and the new owner has the same object address. reset destroys the object after those checks.

sections.title: Address across ownership transfer
paragraphs: Mark the owner before and after move. What do the two Boolean results establish?

reveal.title: Reveal output and trace execution
paragraphs: The log has one creation and one destruction. Two ones prove the old owner is empty and the address matches while the object is alive.

tables.caption: Trace for this run
rows: owner is empty and the address is unchanged.

sections.title: Safe experiments
paragraphs: A log prints create and destroy events; nested blocks reveal reverse destruction order for local objects. Check event counts and owner emptiness after moving rather than dereferencing a released address for an interesting output.

The lab bounds the number of objects and gives each exactly one owner. Draw separate ownership and observation arrows. This will support a small linked list; shared_ptr, the Rule of Five, and deliberate undefined behaviour are not prerequisites here.
Compare addresses while the resource is alive. After reset, look for the destroy line and do not access through observer.

sections.title: Now try your own task
paragraphs: Add an observable mutation after transfer. The destructor must see the new value in the final line.
Write the four-line order for N = 4. Mark separately when the observer ceases to be usable.

selfcheck.prompt: Which log does the shown ownership transfer produce?
options:
create 5
1 1
destroy 5
create 5
0 1
destroy 5
create 5
1 0
destroy 5
feedback: Correct. The unique_ptr moves, while the object does not.
The old unique_ptr is empty after the move.
The live object keeps its address.

selfcheck.prompt: What is guaranteed for unique_ptr p after q=std::move(p)?
options: p is empty and q owns the previous object
selfcheck.feedback: This transfers unique ownership rather than copying the object.
A raw pointer observes rather than owns.

selfcheck.prompt: When is an ordinary local object destroyed?
selfcheck.feedback: RAII ties cleanup to the owner lifetime.

options: No; the owner already manages it
selfcheck.feedback: Manual deletion would violate unique ownership.

selfcheck.feedback: Compare observer with the new owner’s address before reset. After reset, check only the log.

practice.title: Move, modify and release
practice.task: Create an object with value in 0…1000 using make_unique, move its owner, increment value, and release it. Print create N, moved 1 1, value N+1, destroy N+1. Invalid input prints invalid.
criteria: Check N = 0 and N = 1000, then reject a trailing token without printing create.
Transferring ownership does not extend lifetime beyond the final owner.
Do not generalize unique_ptr emptiness to all moved-from types. Never execute dangling access.
Add two cases of your own, including a rejection if the interface allows one. Explain one boundary result.
Keep the source, exact input and observed output.
practice.hint: Compare observer with the new owner’s address before reset. After reset, check only the log.

steps.action: Write the four-line order for N = 4. Mark separately when the observer ceases to be usable.
steps.why: The log lets you verify destruction without reading a destroyed object.
steps.expected: For N=4 the trace is create 4, moved 1 1, value 5, destroy 5.

steps.action: Create the owner, verify transfer, increment through the new owner and call reset.
steps.why: Transfer changes the owner; updating the value requires a separate operation.
steps.expected: The starter prints only create 4 and destroy 4. Completion adds the move check and changed value.

steps.action: Check N = 0 and N = 1000, then reject a trailing token without printing create.
steps.why: Boundary inputs check both the value range and absence of resource creation on rejection.
steps.expected: N=0 and N=1000 each create one object. 4 x rejects before creation.

terms.definition: resource management through object initialization and destruction.
an address or view whose object no longer exists.
a movable but noncopyable unique object owner.
creating an object together with its unique_ptr.
a special function invoked at object lifetime end.
permitting a move operation rather than copying memory by itself.
